position: Whoever fails to do this, though born human, is counted among the unborn, that is, with beasts.
quote: அஃதாவது விலங்கொடு வைத்து எண்ணப்படுவர்.

position: Be compassionate like the great who have reached the state of no further birth.
quote: பிறவா நிலை யெய்திய பெரியோர் போல அருள் உடையவராகுக!

note: Both books make wealth's coming and going a spectacle: the Kural's crowd gathering and dispersing at a show, the Naladiyar's feaster turned beggar.
Both draw the same conclusion from wealth's instability: act on it at once (Kural 333) or share it from the day it comes (here).
The king on the elephant's neck under the royal umbrella appears in both. Here he falls when his deeds turn; in 21 he simply dies like everyone else.
Both urge good deeds before death stops them. The Kural pictures the hiccup that silences the tongue; this quatrain the angry approach of Death.
Both reject 'later': the Kural says virtue is the companion that does not perish when you do, and this quatrain says those who gave first escape Death's road.

Kural 269 says those with the power of austerity can leap past Death (கூற்றம் குதித்தலும்); this quatrain says no one here has leapt past Death and escaped. The conflict holds on Parimelazhagar's literal reading of 269; Kalaignar's figurative 'conquering death' softens it. Mudaliar cites 269 here.
Kural 331 calls taking the impermanent for permanent the lowest புல்லறிவு; this quatrain shows the புல்லறிவாளர் at it, with wealth that flashes and vanishes.
Both say that wealth neither enjoyed nor given is as good as none: in the Kural such a man has nothing, here he is thought to have lost it.
Both say wealth amassed by denying oneself (Kural தற்செற்று, here உடம்பு செற்றும்) and neglecting virtue goes to others. The Naladiyar adds the honey bee as witness.

position: நல்லார் are women, whose affection has waned.
quote: நல்லாரும் - மாதர்களும்.

position: நல்லார் are the learned and good, who have lessened their closeness.
quote: நல்லறிஞரும் நெருக்கம் குறைத்தனர்;

position: அம்மனைக்கோல் is the staff of her own mother.
quote: அம்மனைக் கோல் - அவள் தாயின் ஊன்றுகோல்.

position: Her staff looks to the men like the staff their own mother leaned on, and that pains them.
quote: இவள் ஊன்றும் கைத்தடி, தம் தாய் ஊன்றிய தடிபோல் தெரியும்போது

position: The shoulder-bundle is the stock of good deeds needed for the next world.
quote: தோள் கோட்பு-தோளிற் கோக்கப்படுவது அஃதாவது கட்டுச்சோற்று மூட்டை; இங்கு மறுமைக்கும் வேண்டும். நல்வினைக்கு ஆயிற் றென்க.

note: Here the wise renounce the world even in childhood. Kural 46 asks what a person living household life by virtue would gain by going the outer way. The conflict depends on reading புறத்தாறு as the ascetic path, as Parimelazhagar and Pope do, and துறந்தார் here as world-renunciation, as Shanmuganar does.
Kural 342 says renounce while there is time; this quatrain pushes the right time back to infancy, because age is certain.
Both take the spear-like eye of conventional praise and undo it: 17 by age, which makes it a staff-guided eye, 44 by anatomy, which makes it a scooped-out palm fruit.
Both quote the procrastinator's words, 'we will know it later' (மற்றறிவாம் here, அன்றறிவாம் in the Kural), and reject them. The Naladiyar's reason is that the young die too.

Both use the phrase வீழ்நாள் படா- for a day not lost. In the Kural it is the good deed done daily; here it is the sun that never fails to rise and so measures out a life. The same words point to opposite sides of the account.
Both make the sun the measuring vessel of one's days; in 7 Death does the measuring and eating, in 22 the measure alone is warning enough to do ஒப்புரவு.
The funeral drum sounds in both: in 6 it may sound tomorrow for the hoarder, in 23 it replaces the wedding drum on the same day.
Both treat the life as a temporary occupant of the body, a lodger in the Kural and a dancer in a skin bag here, so the body is not its home.
Both join seeing impermanence to ending the round of births; on Mudaliar's reading of தடுமாற்றம், the wise here resolve to end what Kural 349 says ends when attachment ends.
Both say the rare body must be used to win its fruit before it goes; 34 names that fruit as virtue and adds the sugar-cane image.
Kural 336 says one here yesterday is gone today; this quatrain shrinks the span to a sentence, stood, sat, lay down, gone, and draws the command to act now.
Both picture the life leaving the body as a bird leaving its nest. The Kural makes it a comment on body and life; the Naladiyar applies it to kinsfolk, who leave the body behind for their family.

position: Those who enjoyed the fruit of past virtue and do none in this birth will stand outside in their next birth.
quote: முற்பிறப்பில் செய்த அறத்தால் (தவத்தால்) இன்பம் துய்த்து இப்பிறப்பில் அறம் செய்யாதவர்கள்,

note: Both read present fortune as the visible fruit of virtue: the Kural's palanquin rider and bearer, the Naladiyar's insider and the one at the gate. The Naladiyar adds that the insider's place is lost when the merit is not renewed.
Kural 32 says no ruin exceeds forgetting virtue (மறத்தல்); this quatrain stages the heart that forgets virtue (அறமறந்து) for wealth and asks it what it will do now.
Both make the arrival of past deeds' fruit an occasion for equanimity; the Naladiyar goes further and makes that acceptance the way out of rebirth's confusion.
Both use crushed sugar-cane. In the Kural the base yield only when crushed, a reproach; here the body should be crushed for its juice, a counsel.
Both say virtue gathered in time stays when the body perishes; the Kural calls it an undying companion, the Naladiyar the jaggery kept when the cane refuse burns.
Both turn on not knowing when death comes: the Kural mocks those who plan crores of things without knowing they will live another moment, and this quatrain answers with Death standing behind.
22 urges ஒப்புரவு before one's days end; 37 warns against an ஒப்புரவு done only for the body. Together they mark the word's proper object as others, not oneself.

Both make a small good large: the Kural's millet-sized help counted as a palmyra by those who know its worth, the Naladiyar's banyan seed. The Naladiyar places the growth in the worthiness of the recipient.
Kural 334 says the day looks like a thing but is a saw cutting life, to those who see it; this quatrain describes those who do not see it, and rejoice at each day.

Both argue that keeping the body alive at the cost of dignity buys nothing, since the body does not last: the Kural asks if it is a medicine, the Naladiyar makes the bargain conditional on a body that never dies.

position: The புக்கில் is the body itself, a lodging where the life stays for a while.
quote: துச்சிலை-(உயிரானது ஒதுக்குக் குடியிருக்கும்) வீடாகிய உடம்பின் தன்மையை.

position: The admirers do not know that the body is a paltry shelter.
quote: உடம்பு அற்பமான ஓர் ஒதுக்கிடம் என்பதை அறியார் போலும் !

position: Look at the body as one looks at a bag turned so that the inside faces out.
quote: பை மறியா-பையைப் போல,(உட்பக்கம் வெளிப் பக்கமாம்படி) மாற்றியதாக.

position: Turn the body inside out like a bag and its truth becomes plain.
quote: பையைத் திருப்பிப் பார்ப்பதுபோல் அவ்வுடலைத் திருப்பிப் பார்த்தால் உண்மை விளங்கும்.

note: Both call the body a புக்கில், a lodging; Mudaliar even glosses with துச்சில், the Kural's word. The Kural uses it to show the life has no home of its own; the Naladiyar to show the body is a mean hut not worth desiring.
Kural 80 says a body without love is bone wrapped in skin, implying love makes it more. The Naladiyar treats every body as filth wrapped in skin and allows no such exception.
The water-lily as a figure for the eye appears in both. In Kural 1114 the lover says the lily would bow before her eyes; here the renunciant calls those who make that comparison eyeless.

Kural 1113's lover calls her teeth pearls and her eyes spears; this quatrain calls those who praise teeth as pearls untaught and petty, and answers with bones in the burning ground. The conflict holds if the Kural's Book of Love is read as valuing the lover's praise, not only as dramatised speech.
Kural 913 likens the embrace of women who sell themselves to embracing a corpse in the dark; the Naladiyar extends the corpse to every admired body, which the Kural does not.
In both the skulls laugh and teach: in 49 they speak to all the living, in 50 they cure the infatuated in particular.
Both conclude that the body is not worth valuing: for those ending births even the body is excess in Kural 345, and those cured by the skulls here count themselves as nothing.

position: Austerity here stands for the whole way of renunciation.
quote: தவம் என்றது ஈண்டுத் துறவறத்தின் மேனின்றது.

position: 'Their own work' is austerity, and the endless lore is grammar and mathematics or astrology, tool-sciences studied for a lifetime instead of the way of renunciation.
quote: தங் கருமம்-தமக்கு உறுதியைச் செய்யுந் தொழிலாகிய தவத்தையே

position: The wise do the good deeds fitting for them, and the endless lore is Vedic sastra and astrology.
quote: மேலோர் தமக்கேற்ற நல்வினைகளைச் செய்வர். எனவே, வேத சாத்திரம், சோதிடம் என்றெல்லாம் பிதற்றுகிற

position: The wise weigh, impartially, how small household pleasure is.
quote: இன்பத்தின் சிறுமையை நடுவுநின்று ஆராய்ந்து அறிந்து

position: The wise see that pleasure comes only now and then, a little at a time, and pain is the greater part.
quote: இன்பம் இடையிடையே சிறிதளவு வருவதறிந்தும்

position: The word கடி has both senses, marriage and removal, and the poet invents a reason for the name, a figure Mudaliar calls நிருக்தி.
quote: 'கடி' என்னுஞ் சொற்கு 'மணம்' 'நீக்கு' ஆகிய இரண்டு பொருள்க ளுண்டு.

note: Both make good fortune last only as long as the merit behind it: in 51 evil returns when good deeds are exhausted, and in 93 wealth leaves when the deeds that sent it run out (வினையுலந்தக்கால்).
Mudaliar quotes Kural 266 here: those who do austerity do their own work (தங்கருமம்), and the rest waste themselves. 52 names the waste as endless scholarship.

Kural 397 asks why anyone stays unlearned until death. 52 calls lifelong study of grammar and astrology madness. They are compatible only if the Kural's learning is not the instrumental lore 52 mocks; read together, 52 limits which study is worth a life.
Mudaliar points to 135, where learning has no shore and life is short, so one must choose what to learn. 52 draws the harder conclusion that endless study is folly when death is near.
Both urge renouncing while there is time: 342 says renounce while it is still possible, and 53 has the wise renounce without delay once they see that everything fails to last.

Kural 46 asks what one would gain by leaving a household life lived in virtue. 54 says the wise, seeing the pain in household pleasure, keep off the household way. Both answer whether household life is a path the wise should stay on, and they answer opposite ways. The conflict holds unless 54 is read as describing only the fools' pleasure-seeking household, not a virtuous one.
Both press for the good before the body fails: 335 says do good before the death-rattle stops the tongue, and 55 urges the heart to set out now that youth is gone and age and disease are near.

Kural 52 says a household is nothing if the wife lacks household excellence. 56 starts from the same case and adds that she can't be put away, then draws a conclusion the Kural never draws: marriage itself is to be shunned.
Both make hardship the test of austerity: 267 has the ascetic shine like gold in the fire, and 57 counts as blessed only those who hold their vows when unbearable troubles strike.
Parimelazhagar glosses the pity of Kural 157 (நோநொந்து) by quoting this quatrain: grieving that the wrongdoer may fall into the fiery hell.
Both make control of the five senses the way to release: 24 calls the one who guards the five with firmness a seed for the highest ground, and 59 says the one who steers their craving reaches வீடு.
The two share a line and an argument. 54 ends with leaving household life and 60 with refusing to cling to pleasure as it comes.

Both tie freedom from pain to not craving pleasure: 629 says one who does not want the pleasure within pleasure feels no pain within pain, and 60 has the higher ones see the pain in each pleasure and let it go.
Both find the model of bearing scorn in something below us: 151 in the earth that holds up those who dig it, 61 in the fly that climbs on one's head.

Kural 969 praises those who, like the yak, give up life when honour is lost. 62 says those set on finishing their work don't give up life whenever disgrace comes. Both answer whether disgrace is a reason to die. The conflict holds if 969's மானம் covers the humiliation 62 has in mind; 62 limits itself to those with a task to complete.
Both make speech a burn. In 129 the tongue's burn on the hearer never heals; in 63 careless words burn the speaker without end.
153 calls bearing with the ignorant the strength of strengths; 64 shows the excellent doing it and the base failing at it.
Both count restraint only where it costs something: 301 says one who checks anger where it could take effect truly checks it, and 65 that true patience belongs to one with the power to punish.
65 calls the gift of one without wealth the true gift; 91 promises open doors in the next world to those who give gladly even when they have little.
Both praise bearing the bitter words of those who overstep. 159 likens such people to renunciants in purity; 66 credits their lineage with the restraint.
Both make not returning harm to one who has harmed you the mark of the good. 67 adds that this is not weakness.
Both make the anger of the good brief. Kural 29, in Parimelazhagar's reading, adds that even while it lasts it can't be withstood; 68 stresses only that it cools of itself, leaving out its force.
987 asks what worth is for if it doesn't do good even to those who did harm; 69 says the well-born do exactly that, even to the ungrateful.

position: The friend's lapse is an act done unknowingly, or one that can't be told to others.
quote: தேற்றா ஒழுக்கம் - அறியாச் செய்கை; (பிறர்க்கு) அறிவிக்கக் கூடாச்செய்கை எனினுமாம்.

position: The friend is found in bad conduct.
quote: ஒருவனிடம் தெளியாத தீயொழுக்கம் காணப்படின்

position: One blames oneself either for the bad deeds of a former birth that caused the hurt, or for befriending without first examining the friend.
quote: (அச் செய்கைக்குக் காரணமாகிய தீ வினையை முற்பிறப்பிற் செய்த) தன்னையே எனவும், (முன் நன்கு ஆராயாது அவரொடு நட்புகொண்ட) தன்னையே எனவும் பொருள் கூறுப.

position: Those whose food must not be eaten are the guru, the deity and the poor; he records others who say lower castes or those who serve without love.
quote: உண்ணத்தாகாதார் குரு, தெய்வம், வறிய ராதியர்;

note: Both make getting away from fools a gain: 797 calls leaving a fool's friendship profit, and 71 advises slipping away rather than talking with one.
Both open with the same situation in nearly the same words (நீரல்ல சொல்லியக்கால்): 64 shows the excellent not growing angry, and 72 adds that the world counts retaliation as disgrace.
Both make public regard the measure: 155 says people count those who retaliate as nothing and keep those who forbear like gold, and 72 that the world takes retaliation as disgrace.
784 says friendship exists to rebuke a friend who oversteps, not to laugh together. 73 values those harsh words above an outsider's pleasant ones.
Both use the phrase 'fear what should be feared' (அஞ்சுவது அஞ்சு-): 428 makes it the work of the wise, and 74 lists it among the marks of those who live free of suffering.

Adjacent quatrains on a friend who wrongs you: 75 allows quiet withdrawal once one can bear no more, and 76 forbids abandoning a close friend and says to blame oneself. The conflict holds if both concern the same wrong; it weakens if 75's தேற்றா ஒழுக்கம் is the friend's general misconduct rather than hurt done to oneself.
Both forbid broadcasting a close friend's faults with the same verb (தூற்று-): 188 condemns those who spread even their intimates' faults, and 75 says to withdraw without doing so.
Both hold that close friends are not cast off for the harm they do: 807 says those bound by love keep it even when friends bring ruin, and 76 says to blame oneself rather than leave.
Both say that if one must ask, ask only the right people: 1067 pleads with beggars not to ask those who conceal, and 78 forbids telling one's want to the graceless.
1064 praises the worth that won't consent to begging even with nothing left; 78 implies the same ranking, since only those who lack the resolve to die tell their need at all.
Both put blamelessness above the strongest pull: 656 forbids a deed the worthy would blame even to feed one's starving mother, and 79 forbids blameworthy pleasure even if it would never end.
Both refuse to let ruin excuse wrongdoing: 205 says not to do evil because one is poor, and 80 says not to plot the ruin of the worthy even when one is ruined oneself.

position: Because it doesn't come out but stays within and subsides only after great suffering, the desire of the wise is called very cruel.
quote: வெளிப்பட்டொழியாது உள்ளே நின்று மிக வருந்தி அடங்குதலின், அறிவுடையார் காமம் மிகவுங் கொடிது எனப்படுத லுணர்க.

note: 146 lists four things that never leave the adulterer: enmity, sin, fear and blame. 82 keeps the same four and pairs them with four goods he loses: virtue, renown, friendship and greatness.
148 calls not looking at another's wife great manliness (பேராண்மை); 84 calls the act unmanliness (ஆணின்மை).
Both turn on the look (நோக்கு): 148 praises the manliness that does not look at another's wife, and 86 asks why a married man would look at all.

In 1134 the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness. In 88 the strong, fearing shame, keep desire hidden until it subsides. Both make claims about whether shame can hold desire, and they answer opposite ways. The conflict depends on reading 1134 as a general claim; it is a lover's plea in the Book of Love, while 88 states a rule about the strong.
Both contrast an outer burn with an inner one: in 129 the fire's wound heals but the tongue's scar does not, and in 89 arrow, fire and sun burn the body while desire burns the mind.
Both say desire burns where fire can't: 1159 says fire burns only when touched while love burns at a distance, and 90 that fire can be escaped in water but desire can't.
The same figure in another domain: 1049 says one can sleep in the midst of fire but not of poverty, and 90 that one can escape fire but not desire. Each makes fire the lesser affliction.

position: The doors are those of the other world, which Pope calls heaven.
quote: ஆண்டைக்கதவு-அவ்வுலகத்துக் கதவுகள்.

position: The doors are those of release (வீடுபேறு), not of a heaven.
quote: வீடுபேற்றுக் கதவுகள் அடைக்கப்படாவாம்.

position: உம்மை means 'in a former birth': those who did not give then are the poor with unlit hearths now.
quote: உம்மை- முற்பிறப்பில். என்பர்-என்றிகழப்படுவர்;

position: உம்மை means 'you': the poor with unlit hearths will scorn you as misers.
quote: கொடாத கருமிகள் என்று உம்மை இழித்து உரைப்பர்.

position: The word is 'he gave', spoken by the worthy about a giver.
quote: சான் றோரால் கொடுத்தார் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்லையோவெனில்;

position: The word is praise that the worthy themselves gave.
quote: பெரியார் கொடுத்தார் எனப்படும் புகழ்ச் சொல்லையோ,

note: Both hold that giving does not wait for wealth: 218 says those who know their duty don't falter in helping even when means are gone, and 91 rewards those who give gladly when they have little.
Both argue from impermanence: 333 says wealth does not stay, so do what lasts at once, and 92 says death, age and disease are near, so share while wealth is in hand.

Both deny that guarding keeps wealth: 376 says what is not one's own won't stay however it is guarded, and 93 that wealth leaves when its merit runs out however tightly held. 376 names fate; 93 names past deeds.

Both explain the many poor by what was not done: 270 by the few who practise austerity, and 94 in Mudaliar's reading by the failure to give in a former birth. They give different causes for the same fact without denying each other.
Both put a number on not begging: 1061 says it is worth ten million times more even when givers are glad, and 95 that it is worth twice as much as giving.
Both put the giver's wealth in a fruiting tree at the town's centre, where all can reach it.
1008 keeps the tree in the town's centre but makes the miser's wealth a poison tree fruiting there; 96 moves the miser's barren palm out to the burning ground.
211 makes the rain the model of help that seeks no return. 97 sets rain and the good's giving side by side as the two things the world can't survive without.
In 19 giving depends on rain: if the sky fails, giving and austerity cease. In 97 the two are parallel supports, each needed on its own.
Both say giving to those who can repay is not giving but lending: 221 calls it a measured return (குறியெதிர்ப்பை), and 98 a profitable loan (பொலிகடன்).
Both turn on small things adding up: in 475 peacock feathers, piled high enough, break a cart's axle, and in 99 small gifts fill the bowl. One warns, the other encourages.
Both make giving the source of lasting praise: 232 says all that speakers praise rests on those who give to the asker, and 100 that the word 'they gave' is heard through three worlds.

position: The உறுவர் are sages, and destined pleasures can no more be prevented than destined pains.
quote: அன்ன ஆம்-அத் தன்மையவேயாம்; 'நீக்கல் ஆகா' என்றபடி.

position: No strong person can stop what fate brings, and no one can obtain by their own effort what they wish to gain.
quote: பெற விரும்புகிறவற்றைத் தாமாகப் பெறுவதென்பதும் அதுபோன்றே இயலாததாம்

note: Both make a deed's consequence inseparable from its doer, with different images: the Kural's ruin stays at the heels like a shadow, and the Naladiyar's deed goes looking like a calf for its mother.
101 says the deed finds its doer among many; 120 says it is the only thing that goes with him at death. Together they make the deed both pursuer and sole companion.
Both draw the same conclusion from impermanent wealth: do the lasting good at once. 102 adds beauty, youth and standing to the list and condemns the life that does nothing.
Both say that enjoyment is measured out in advance: the Kural even for those who amass millions, the Naladiyar for all who want prosperity.

On Mudaliar's reading, 104 says that even sages cannot remove what is bound to befall. 269 says that those who attain the power of austerity can even leap past death. Both concern whether ascetic power can overcome what is coming; the tension holds if உறுவர் are ascetics and 269's கூற்றம் is fated death.

104 says no one can remove what is destined, as no one can make rain fall; 620 says those who strive without flagging see even fate's back. The tension depends on reading 620 as effort overcoming fate, as Pope and Kalaignar do.
Both describe the great brought low and give the same cause: in 3 the elephant-riders fall when their deeds are spent, and in 105 the palm-sized become millet-sized through former deeds.
Both deny that the unlearned truly live: the Kural says they can only be said to exist, like barren land, and the Naladiyar says Death will not even take them, as husks.

107 makes begging the outworking of the beggar's own former deeds, so the order that produces it is just. 1062 calls down ruin on whoever ordained that anyone should live by begging, treating it as an unjust order. The tension depends on 107's vinai being the beggar's own deeds.
Both describe one who knows and still does wrong. The Kural calls him the greatest fool; the Naladiyar traces the act to former deeds, which explains it without removing the blame.
Both say that a person's will has no say in what comes: in the Kural, care cannot keep what is not one's own; here, wishing cannot keep off what is due.
Both end a chapter on fate by asking why anyone grieves when the bad arrives, since it is as fixed as the good.
The Kural makes killing a kindness received the sin with no escape. On both commentators' reading, 111 names something worse: a promise held out and then broken.
223 praises never uttering 'I have nothing' and giving instead. 111 allows that saying 'no' is blameless when one truly cannot give; the fault lies in false promising.

112 says the worthy and unworthy never fall from their natures at any time. 514 says that many people, though trusted after every test, change through the nature of the work. The tension holds if 514 means people really change, as Parimelazhagar says, rather than that the tests misjudged them.
113 observes that kin vanish in trouble; 796 turns that into a benefit, saying ruin is a rod that measures one's people.
Both say that whoever secures wealth gets the other two aims of life as well. The Naladiyar adds the cost of failing: suffering like being boiled.

114 makes wealth the key to virtue and pleasure; 1, opening the book, shows the rich reduced to begging for gruel and says wealth should not be counted on. Wealth secures the other two only while it lasts.
Both say that the poor are not heard however sound their words. The Naladiyar adds the other half: the rich are heard even when unlearned.
Both describe study that leaves a person unrestrained. The Kural calls such a person the greatest fool; the Naladiyar says it is their nature, as bitterness is the gourd's.

117 says to scorn those who scorn you; 151 says that bearing with them, as the earth bears those who dig it, is the highest thing. Both concern the same situation. The tension depends on reading 117 as advice, as Mudaliar, Shanmuganar and Pope do, and not as irony.

Within the Naladiyar: 72 says that when unworthy people speak improperly, bearing it in silence is fitting and the world thinks retaliation shameful. 117 says to scorn the scorners first. The tension holds if 117's scorners and 72's speakers are the same kind of person.
118 says virtue is one in nature whatever form its ways take. 34 says what that one thing is: a spotless mind, everything else being show.
36 makes virtue the companion that does not die with you. 120 says the only thing that goes along is the deed, which includes bad deeds; so the companion can also be a burden.

position: The sorrow in which people linger is household life itself; Mudaliar also says the verse rejects meat-eating.
quote: துக்கத்துள் - துன்பமாகிய இல்வாழ்க்கையில்.

position: The sorrow is the world's suffering in general, in which people are bewildered.
quote: உலகத் துன்பத்துள் மயங்கித் துறவுநெறியைக் கொள்ளாத மக்களின்

position: ஆக்கம் means joining the unlearned, and that association is what burns.
quote: (கல்லார்கண்) ஆக்கம் - (பேதையரிடத்து) ஆகுதல், அஃதாவது சேர்தல்;

position: ஆக்கம் is one's own growth, which friendship with the unlearned burns up in both worlds.
quote: இம்மையிலும் மறுமையிலும் தம் வளர்ச்சியைச் சுட்டழிக்கு மாதலால்

note: On Mudaliar's reading, 121 makes household life itself the sorrow in which those who fail to renounce end as corpses. 46 asks what anyone would gain by leaving a household life lived in virtue for the other path. The tension depends on Mudaliar's gloss of துக்கம்; on Shanmuganar's it is weaker.
Both condemn eating flesh. The Kural asks how one who fattens his flesh on others' can have grace; the Naladiyar makes his belly a burning ground.
Both say harm done to others returns to the doer. The Naladiyar makes the return copy the harm: those who caged birds wear irons.
Both explain a wretched diseased body as the result of having taken life. The Naladiyar names the creature and the disease.
Both say a person takes on the nature of their company, the Kural with water changing with the soil and the Naladiyar with ghee turning to flame.

112 says the worthy never fall from their nature, as jaggery is never bitter. 124 says even the upright turn to cruel deeds when they join the wicked. Both concern whether good character can be changed; the tension holds if 124's கோடார் are truly good, as Mudaliar's நடுவுநிலைமையுடையார் implies.
124 shows company corrupting the upright; 139 shows it improving the unlearned, like a new pot taking on the scent of flowers. The same mechanism works in both directions.
Both use the waxing and waning moon for good and bad friendship. The Kural sets the wise against fools, and the Naladiyar the great against the small.
Both warn of friendship formed without examination; the Kural says it ends in mortal grief, the Naladiyar finds a snake where sandal was expected.

127 says no one can know another's mind, because minds and deeds differ. 706 says the face shows what is uppermost in the heart, as crystal shows what is near it. The tension depends on taking 127 as a general claim rather than a warning about deceivers.
702 grants that someone may know another's mind without doubt, but calls such a person equal to a god. 127 says no one has that power, which agrees that it is beyond ordinary people.
Both describe friendship without inner consent. The Kural calls it an anvil waiting for the right moment to strike; the Naladiyar says it becomes a stain.
Both use a bright sword in the wrong hands. In the Kural it is learning held by one who fears the assembly; in the Naladiyar it is one's own strength lost through association with the unlearned.
Both prefer distance from fools to closeness: the Kural rates the enmity of the wise far above a fool's intimacy, and the Naladiyar says the good course is to get away from the unlearned.

61 says no gain is known greater than children who learn what should be known. 130 rebukes the heart for pining for children and says there is no gain for the soul but good done. The tension softens if 61 speaks of worldly gains and 130 only of the soul's.

position: True beauty is learning held together with conduct that lets one judge fairly that one has not strayed from virtue.
quote: ஒழுக்கத்தோடு கல்வியுடைமையும் பெற்றிருத்தலே அழகு என்பது கருத்து.

position: Learning is true beauty because it produces the impartial quality of being good at heart.
quote: நடுநிலைப் பண்பை உண்டாக்குவதால் கல்வி அழகே உண்மை அழகு

position: Learning does not perish for as long as its owner lives.
quote: தாம் உளர் ஆ - தாம் உயிருள்ளவராக வாழுமளவும். கேடு இன்று - அழிதலில்லை.

position: Learning makes its owner live on forever through fame and does not perish.
quote: தம்மைப்புகழால் என்றும் உள்ளவராக்கி அழியாது நிற்கும்

note: Both deny that outward beauty is worth anything without learning: the Kural compares it to a well-made clay doll, and the Naladiyar refuses it the name of beauty.
Both say learning does not perish when other possessions do. The Naladiyar spells out the ways it differs from wealth.

On Mudaliar's reading, 132 says learning lasts as long as its owner lives; 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven. Shanmuganar's reading, that it lasts through fame, is closer to the Kural's.
Both rank the low-born learned above the unlearned, the Kural by comparing them to the high-born unlearned and the Naladiyar with salt from brackish soil.

133 sets the low-born learned in the highest place; 142 says excellence, gentleness and good conduct belong only to the high-born, whatever wealth others gain. Read together, learning can raise one's rank but, in 142, not those qualities.
Both make learning the best thing a father gives his children: the Kural as a place at the front of the assembly, the Naladiyar as an inheritance that cannot be taken.
Both insist on learning what is to be learned. The Naladiyar adds the reason: learning is endless and life is short.

Both say the worth of what is taught does not depend on who teaches it: the Kural says to see the truth in whatever is heard from anyone, and the Naladiyar says to learn from the learned whatever their caste.
Both make the meeting of the learned a delight. The Kural describes how they part; the Naladiyar ranks their gathering above heaven.
Both say that friendship with people of character grows sweeter with time, the Kural like a book reread and the Naladiyar like cane eaten from the tip.
Both say understanding takes on the nature of one's company, the Kural with water and soil and the Naladiyar with water and flowers.
Both make the purpose of learning the perception of what is true, which leads out of rebirth on Mudaliar's reading of 140. The Naladiyar adds that worldly learning cannot do this.

position: The closing question is ironic: high birth brings no gain of its own, since good is credited to birth and evil is loudly blamed.
quote: எல்லாம் உணர்ந்த உயர்குடியில் பிறந்ததால் அவருக்குச் சொந்த நன்மை என்னவோ?

note: Both use an animal that will not go against its nature in extremity: the yak that dies when it loses a hair, and the lion that will not eat grass. The Kural speaks of honour, the Naladiyar of the principles of the well-born.

Both name three qualities the well-born never lose. The Kural's are conduct, truthfulness and shame; the Naladiyar's are fullness of character, gentleness and conduct, and it adds that wealth cannot buy them.
Both say a fault in the well-born is seen by everyone, the Kural like the spot on the moon and the Naladiyar as blame spread by many.
Both call people who lack a human moral quality trees or wood: in the Kural those without courtesy, however sharp, and in the Naladiyar the low-born who lack the four fears.
Both say a moral fear or shame is found naturally only in the well-born.
Both list four qualities of a good lineage, and both include giving and sweet speech.

146 says that good company, sweet speech, giving and goodness of mind are found only among the well-born. 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction comes from the deeds one does. The two disagree about whether excellence follows birth or deeds. The tension holds if 972's distinction means worth of character, as Pope and Kalaignar take it, and if 146's qualities belong to that worth.
219 says that, for a good man, poverty is being unable to do what should be done. 147 says the well-born still do it even in hardship, so for them poverty in that sense never fully arrives.
The two share the phrase ஒப்புரவிற்கு ஒல்கார்: those who know their duty, or the well-born, do not slacken in serving others when they lack the means. The Naladiyar adds the half-eclipsed moon.
Both say the base do not give even when they could: in the Kural they won't shake off their wet hands for anyone but those who would break their jaws.
Both say that the well-born keep their generous nature when their means have shrunk.

position: Because the moon is specified as the moon in the wide sky, the 'noble' of the chapter title are to be taken as the high-born.
quote: 'மேன்மக்கள்' உயர் குடிப் பிறப்புடையார் என்பது குறிப்பிற் கொள்க

note: Both use the spot on the moon. In 957 the fault of the well-born shows as plainly as the moon's spot; in 151 the noble differ from the moon in being unable to live with the spot at all.
Both make honour a matter of life and death: in 969 the honourable give up life like the yak that loses its hair, and in 151 the noble waste away at a single stain.
Aim high regardless of outcome: 596 says a lofty aim, even if thwarted, keeps its worth, and 152 says the arrow that misses a lion beats the one that kills a jackal.
Want does not license wrongdoing. 656 holds even if one's mother starves; 153 holds even when one's own body is reduced to sinew.
785 says long acquaintance is not needed for friendship, only shared feeling; 154 shows the worthy treating a single meeting as an old bond.

791 warns that nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry, since the true friend cannot later withdraw. 154 praises binding someone seen once as if an old friend. The tension holds if 154 means any passer-by; Pope's parenthetical '(worthy) men' softens it, but the Tamil has no such qualifier.
153 calls bearing with fools the strength of strengths; 155 shows that strength as patient listening to an ignorant speaker so as not to shame him.
403 puts the burden on the unlearned: they are good if they stay silent before the learned. 155 takes the case where they do not, and puts the burden on the learned to endure it kindly.
Both use crushed sugar-cane, to opposite ends. In 1078 the base are like cane, giving only when crushed; in 156 the well-born are like cane, still sweet however crushed.
159 makes bearing harsh words from the insolent as pure as renunciation; 156 makes it the mark of good birth.
Both say the virtuous cannot speak evil even by a slip: வழுக்கியும் in 139, தள்ளியும் in 157.
148 calls not looking at another's wife both virtue and complete conduct; 158 makes that blindness one of three abstentions that leave nothing more to teach.

Both give one abstention near-sufficient moral weight: 181 says it is good to be called one who does not backbite even if one does wrong, and 158 counts silence in backbiting among the restraints that make virtue-teaching unnecessary.
224 admits that being asked is painful until one sees the asker's glad face; 159 describes the excellent as treating the prospect of being asked as good from the outset.
1057 is the asker's side: the heart rejoices at givers who do not scorn. 159 is the giver's side: the excellent honour those who may ask instead of scorning them.
443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of all things; 160 calls meeting the well-born a treasure cave, against the base who chase the rich.

position: The 'great' whose anger cannot be escaped are kings.
quote: பெருமையுடையார் செறின்- பெருமை யுடைய‌ அர‌ச‌ர் கோப்பிப்பாராயின்

position: The great are elders in general, angered by someone who has wronged them.
quote: பிழை செய்தவரைப் பெரியவர் சினந்தால்

note: 700 warns a minister that doing improper things on the strength of long familiarity with the king brings ruin. 161 makes the same point about presuming on the forbearance of the great.
896 says one may survive fire but not a lasting offence against the great; 161 says the damage of offending them cannot be undone.
443 calls winning the great the rarest of things. 162 imagines that rarity handed over free and wasted by people who cannot use it.
Both locate worth in the judgment of the worthy. 163 dismisses the verdict of the base, and 165 dismisses one's own verdict on oneself.
895: those who have drawn a fierce king's anger exist nowhere, wherever they go. This matches Mudaliar's reading of 164, where the angered great are kings.
900: even those with overwhelming support perish if the eminent are angered. This matches the reading of 164 in which the great are the morally great and the fortress is no defence.
978 says smallness adorns itself by admiring itself; 165 gives the words of that self-admiration and denies it the name of esteem.
The same claim with a different measure of time: 782 has the waxing and waning moon, 166 the shortening and lengthening shadow.

691 advises those who serve kings to stay neither too near nor too far, like people warming at a fire. 167 observes that those who stay close are the ones who enjoy a king's wealth, without the warning.

839 says, with irony, that friendship with fools is sweet because parting from them brings no pain. 168 says parting even from the undiscerning brings great sorrow. The two make opposite claims about the pain of parting from fools, if தெரிவிலார் is read as fools, as Mudaliar's gloss அறிவிலார் has it.

Both end with கோடி உறும். 816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool, a ranking of companions. 168 drops the ranking: mixing with no one is ten million times better.

168 concludes that not mixing with anyone is far better because of the pain of parting. 174 says no one would hate even painful birth if they could keep friendship with the noble. One makes withdrawal the remedy for life's pain, the other makes companionship the remedy.

Both count days: 38 says letting no day fall idle without good blocks the road of births, and 169 says the good have no day without learning, visiting the great or giving. Both use படாஅ for days that do not occur.
Both define greatness as bowing: பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை in 978, பெரியார் பெருமை சிறுதகைமை in 170.
226 says removing the hunger of the destitute is where one should store wealth; 170 says only those who relieve their dependants' distress are truly wealthy.

position: கேடு is harm or misfortune in general.
quote: கேடும் - தீங்கும்

position: கேடு is death, completing the list of separation, illness and death.
quote: கொடிய பிணியும் சாவும்

position: குலம் is the company one joins, keeping the verse within the chapter's theme.
quote: த‌ம்த‌ம் குல‌ம் ந‌ல‌த்தால் - தாந்தாஞ் சேர்கிற‌ கூட்ட‌த்தின் நன்மையான்

position: குலம் is the family one is born into; the worthy are formed by their birth.
quote: தாம் பிறந்த குடியின் பெருமையால் உயர்ந்தோர் உருவாகின்றனர்

note: 455 says purity of mind and deed both lean on purity of company; 171 shows company acting on past deeds as well, clearing the faults of youth.
415 calls the words of the good a staff on slippery ground; 172 closes its six precepts with taking in the words of the great every day.
Both commend bearing others' harsh words; 159 ranks those who do it with renunciants, 172 lists it among the basic precepts.
Both treat birth as the thing to escape: 362 says if one must want, want not to be born, and 173 seeks out those who know birth is bitter.
173 declares birth bitter from the start. 174, placed next to it, grants that and adds that friendship with the good makes birth something no one would resent.
460 says there is no greater support than good company. 174 raises the stakes: good company is what reconciles a person to being born at all.

Both use water changed by what it joins. In 452 water takes on the nature of its soil, as a mind takes on its company; in 175 sewage takes the name of the sacred river, as the lowly take the standing of the good.
Both use the moon's dark spot. In 151 the moon tolerates its flaw and the noble cannot; in 176 the flaw is worshipped because it sits in the moon.
Milk and its mixture, in opposite directions: in 1000 good milk is spoiled by a bad vessel, as wealth by a graceless owner; in 177 water is absorbed into milk, as the small into the great.
446: enemies can do nothing to one who walks with the worthy. 178 gives the image of grass the plough cannot uproot because it grows against a stump.
458 says that even the worthy, whose minds are good, are protected by good company. 179 gives the converse: their worth is wrecked by bad company.
453 says what a person is called comes from their company; 180 says the pure in mind are scorned because of theirs.
The same mechanism run both ways: in 177 the mean are hidden by the great, in 180 the pure are blackened by the bad.

position: The supports that fail are the attachments of household life.
quote: அ சார்பு- (இல்வாழ்க்கையாகிய) அப் பற்றுக்கள்

position: Toward liars, one should be wholly a speaker of lies.
quote: சால சலமே-மிகவும் பொய்யே பேசுதற்கும்

note: 1050 says the destitute who do not renounce merely consume salt and gruel. 181 has someone who can no longer give conclude that renunciation is the fitting course.
331 calls taking the impermanent for permanent the lowest understanding; 182 gives the example of the householder who thinks himself settled for good.

46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household life for the ascetic way. 182 calls those content in home life fools and praises those who see its supports as passing. The conflict holds on Mudaliar's reading, where the failing supports are household attachments themselves; if 182 targets only heedlessness, the two are compatible.
Both urge good deeds now because the body may fail without warning: 335 before the death-hiccup stops the tongue, 183 because the body changes without cause.
Both use a village water source for the generous: 215 compares a wise man's wealth to a full town tank, 184 compares the great in decline to a spring-fed well that still serves in drought.
218 says those who know their duty do not slacken in serving others even when they have no means; 184 says the great keep giving in decline.
Consecutive water images for giving in decline: a spring-fed well in 184, a dry riverbed that yields to digging in 185.
Both end with செய்வர் செயற்பாலவை. In 153 the poor worthy do their duty within their means; in 185 the once-rich keep doing it after ruin, for fewer people.
955: even when what they can give has shrunk, an old family keeps its nature. 185 says the same of the ruined giver who still gives to a few.
957 says a fault in the well-born stands out like the moon's spot; 186 says the same with a brand on a white bull, and adds that the crimes of the small go unseen.
816: being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than intimacy with a fool. 187 goes further: even enmity with the wise brings dignity, while intimacy with the mean brings grief.

987 asks what worth is for if it cannot do good even to those who do harm. 188 says to meet foes with terror and the false with falseness. The conflict is direct on Mudaliar's reading of சலவர் as liars; on Pope's reading the third clause is milder, but the clause on foes still conflicts.
830 advises friendship of the face, not the heart, with a foe who turns friendly. 188 likewise answers each person in their own coin rather than with uniform goodness.
360 says suffering ends when desire, anger and delusion perish. On Shanmuganar's reading of the three faults, 190 offers a practice that removes them: feeding others before oneself.
227: hunger does not touch one who habitually shares food. 190 says sharing the first-served food keeps the worthy from sorrow till the end.

position: The other kin live without hardship on what the energetic one gives.
quote: கொடுப்பதை உண்டு மற்ற சுற்றத்தார்கள் துன்பின்றி வாழ்வர்

position: The Mutharaiyar were best taken as a generous patron of the poet's own time.
quote: முத்தரையரென்பார் ஆசிரியர் காலத்திருந்த கொடை வள்ள லொருவ ரெனக் கோடலே சிறப்புடைத் தென்க

note: 615 calls the one who prefers work to pleasure a pillar who wipes away his kin's troubles. On Shanmuganar's reading of 191, kin rest easy on what the energetic one provides.
611 says effort brings the greatness the task requires; 192 shows it as a twig hardening into a post strong enough for an elephant.
618 says bad fortune is no disgrace but failing to work is; 193 tells the knowledgeable not to scorn humble work when fortune is thin.
198 says the lion-hearted would die rather than do anything disgraceful; 193 says even the tiger eats a frog when hungry. Read together, humble work is not disgrace, and dishonourable deeds are.
619 says effort pays its wage even when fate denies the goal; 194 makes persistence through failure the very definition of manliness.
Both begin from success or failure (இசையும் எனினும் இசையாதெனினும் in 152, இசையாதெனினும் in 194) and judge a person by how they act regardless of outcome.
972: birth is alike for all beings, and distinction differs by the work done. 195 says good and bad caste are mere words and lineage is made by austerity, learning and effort.

951 says integrity and shame exist together naturally only in the well-born. 195 says good and bad lineage are words without substance. Both concern whether birth carries real moral qualities, and they answer opposite ways unless 951's இற்பிறந்தார் is read as a lineage made by conduct, as 195 defines it.

On Shanmuganar's reading of 179, the worthy are formed by the family they are born into, as paddy by its soil; 195 says good and bad lineage are only words. On Mudaliar's reading of குலம் in 179 as one's company, there is no conflict.
663 says true manliness lets a deed be known only when finished, since revealing it midway brings grief; 196 says the perceptive keep their plans to themselves until the work is done.
701 calls one who reads what is unsaid an ornament to the world; 196 says the world is under the sign of those who read others' drive from their features.
Both picture a structure eaten at the base and propped up. In 1030 a family whose foot is cut by trouble falls if no good person props it; in 197 the son props the decaying father like banyan roots.
70 says a son repays his father by making people wonder what penance the father did. 197 gives a more practical repayment: covering the father's weakness when he falters.
656: even seeing one's mother starve, do not do what the worthy condemn. 198: even dying in want at home, the strong do not do what brings disgrace.
Both set death against dishonour: 969's yak dies when it loses its hair, 198's lion-hearted would die in want rather than be disgraced.
601 says the lamp of lineage dies when sloth covers it; 199 says high birth is worth nothing without great manliness, like a flower that has lost its scent.
Nearly the same claim: 1065 says even watery gruel got by one's own effort (தாள்தந்தது) is the sweetest food, and 200 says water won by one's own effort (தாளாண்மை) becomes nectar.

In 200 the Mutharaiyar are patrons whose feasts the base enjoy; in 296 the poor who never go begging to the rich are themselves called Mutharaiyar. The patron's name moves from giver to the self-reliant.

position: Those who enter the fire are loving kin.
quote: ந‌ட்டார் - அன்புடை உற‌வின‌ர்.

position: Those who enter the fire are true friends.
quote: உண்மை நண்பர் எனப்படுவார், பொருளோடு நெருப்பிலே நிற்கும் உலையாணிக்கோல் போல

note: 521 says that only kin keep honouring old ties when a man has lost everything; 201 describes what that loyalty does inside the sufferer, likening it to a mother forgetting the pains of birth.
Both make the good man a fruiting tree that the many enjoy. 216 says his wealth is like a tree ripening in the middle of town; 202 adds the shade tree and insists he toils for it himself.
Both put the burden of those who depend on a household on its capable members: 1027 compares them to the brave in battle, 203 to a branch that never fails to bear its own fruit.
Both contrast a friendship that holds or grows with one that soon fails; 782 uses the waxing and waning moon, 204 the ascetic's unswerving path.

Both distrust speech that labels a relation, and their wording is close (இனையர், இன்னர்/இன்னம்). 790 says friendship looks shabby when friends describe what they are to each other; 205 says the best people never sort others into ours and theirs.

Both say that plain gruel (கூழ், புற்கை) shared with one's own is sweeter than the finest food. The Kural says it is sweeter than ambrosia when one's children's little hands have stirred it; 206 says it is sweeter than a golden-dish feast from those who are not one's own.
The kin chapter and the chapter on testing friendship use the same contrast of poor food given with love and rich food given without it. 217 ends in the bitter strychnos fruit, 206 and 210 in neem.

Both say that hospitality without warmth spoils the meal for the guest. 90 says a guest withers like the anicham flower at an averted face; 207 says the punctual feast in an unloving house tastes of neem.
Both single out those who leave when ruin comes: 208 compares them to tongs that let go in the fire, and 799 says the memory of such friends burns the heart at the hour of death.
787 defines friendship partly as sharing the suffering in ruin; 209 says a friendship that shares only joys can do nothing even in the next world.

position: The sweetness the second group lacks is the sweetness of learning.
quote: கல்வியறி வாகிய இனிய தன்மை யில்லாதவர்களது நட்பு

position: The sweetness they lack is a sweet disposition, as Pope also has it.
quote: என்றும் இனிய பண்பு இல்லாதவாது நட்போ

note: A near doublet: both compare friendship with the learned to eating sugarcane from the tip and the other kind to eating it from the root. 138 ends on those without character or kindness, 211 on those without sweetness.
Both say friendship with the right people grows sweeter with use. 783 compares it to a book whose delight grows with study; 211 to sugarcane eaten from the tip.

212 relies on family as the only workable guarantee that a friend won't change, since minds can't be known. 245 says people are not like their இனம் but like their minds. The tension holds if 245's இனம் includes family, as Mudaliar's 'இனத்தார்' allows; if it means only the company one keeps, the two are about different things.
793 tells one to know a man's qualities, family, faults and connections before befriending him. 212 keeps family but doubts the rest: the mind can't be known, so family is the one dependable ground.

Both prize love that survives injury from the friend: 807 says those bound by love don't stop loving even when the friend ruins them, and 213 pictures the dog wagging its tail with the spear in its body.
Both say that a shared heart, not meeting or long acquaintance, makes friendship. 214 adds the reverse case: long absence doesn't break it.
Both use a flower's opening and closing for inconstant friendship. 425 says understanding is not opening and closing; 215 contrasts tree flowers that stay open with pond flowers that close.
104 says those who know its value count a millet-sized help as palmyra-sized. On Mudaliar's reading the palmyra in 216 stands for the best friends, who form a great friendship from one small help.

Both prefer hostility from the right people to friendship with the wrong. 187 says the enmity of the wise brings dignity; 219 says enmity is better than the friendship of those without clear understanding.
816 says being a stranger to the wise is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool. 219 goes further: open enmity is better than a fool's friendship.
Both argue for testing before befriending because a formed bond can't be cleanly undone. 791 gives the reason as the friend's own loyalty; 220 gives it as the pain of parting, even from a snake.
Both say parting from a bad bond still hurts. 168 concludes that it is best to mix with no one; 220 concludes that one must test long before mixing.

position: One is to honour them more than one's real friends, with no suggestion of pretence.
quote: த‌ம‌ரினும் ந‌ன்கு ம‌தித்து - ந‌ண்ப‌ரினும் மிக‌க் கௌர‌வித்து

position: The honour is an outward show while the truth is kept inside.
quote: தம் உறவினரினும் நன்கு மதிப்பது போல் வெளிக்குக் காட்டி

note: 75 says to bear a friend's unkind conduct as far as one can and, if one cannot, to withdraw without speaking ill. 221 offers no such exit: keep them and keep their faults inside.
Both ask for a charitable account of a friend's wrongs. 805 says to put them down to folly or great intimacy; 221 says every good thing has its husk.
Both make forbearance toward those who damage you an image from the land: the earth bears those who dig into it (151), and the farmer re-dams the stream that keeps breaking through (222).
803 asks what use an old friendship is if one doesn't accept a friend's liberties as one's own acts. 223 puts the same demand as a maxim: one person's patience keeps two in friendship.
Both picture a wrong friendship as burning the heart. In 799 it is the memory of friends who deserted one; in 224 it is a friend one cannot leave who lacks good nature.
Adjacent quatrains turn fire both ways: in 224 a bad friend is a fire lit to burn the heart, and in 225 the fire that burned the house is still needed daily, so the friend who hurt one is kept.
Both forbid casting off a close friend for the hurt they cause. 76 says to blame oneself, since even beasts find parting hard; 226 says no one cuts off the hand that poked their eye.
980 says greatness hides others' faults and smallness only tells them. 227 applies this to friends and ranks the teller below the wrongdoer.
188 asks what those who spread the faults of their intimates would do to strangers. 227 makes the same judgement on those who publish a friend's wrongs.
Both reinterpret a friend's hurtful act. 805 reads it as folly or intimacy; 228 says it becomes good once held in the heart.

830 says to befriend a former enemy with the face, let go in the heart, and then drop the friendship. 229 also hides an inner judgement behind outward regard, but toward a friend who has proved false, and it never says to drop him.

504 tells one to examine a person's qualities and faults and take what predominates. 230 forbids that examination once the friendship is made, so the two divide the labour: examine before, never after.

Both are first-person curses with the same frame: may I go where the worst betrayer of a friend goes, while the world laughs. 230 names the one who did not keep a friend's secret, and 238 the one who violated a friend's wife.

position: உருவிற்கு அமைந்தான் is first one with some qualities fit for greatness; Mudaliar gives good looks only as another view.
quote: பெருமைக்குரிய சில நற்குணங்களுடையா-னிடத்தே

position: It is one handsome in form, as Pope also has it.
quote: உருவத்தில் அழகாய் அமைந்திருப்பவனிடம்

note: Both describe friends who stay while there is something to gain. 812 asks what it matters whether one keeps or loses them; 231 shows them putting up with discomfort until their business is done.
284 has crowds gathering like crows while wealth lasts and no one asking after you when it goes; 231 shows the same self-interest from inside the friendship.
Both say the friendship of the worthless is barren even at its fullest. 811 says it is better shrinking than growing; 232 says even at its height it is like failed rain.
Both set the company of the learned against heaven. 137 doubts heaven could be sweeter; 233 makes the comparison explicit and adds that bad company is one of the hells.
Both put the company one keeps at the extremes: no greater support than good company and no greater affliction than bad (460), heaven and hell (233).
Both describe a friendship that seems to grow and then shrinks: the moon past full (782), fire in straw (234).
818 says to let slip the friendship of those who make difficulties of what they could do. 235 names the same delay, with empty promising, and says it brings suffering even to ascetics.

177 says the smallness of the small stops showing when they join the great, as water in milk looks like milk. 236 says their deeds stay different though they grow up beside the great. Read together, association changes how the small look, not what they do.

Both say an outside good doesn't change an inner nature: 823 says the unworthy rarely become good at heart however many good books they study, and 236 says the same of their friendship with the large-natured.
Both make inner accord the condition of friendship. 825 says not to trust the words of those not one with you in mind; 237 says friendship with them is painful.
787 says friendship shares the suffering when ruin comes. 238 raises the stake to one's own life and curses the friend who holds back.
797 calls leaving the friendship of fools a gain. 239 describes the reverse exchange, leaving the discerning for the petty-minded, as ghee swapped for neem oil.

240 says the discerning who take up with bad company are ruined; 244 says the good-natured don't turn bad in mind though their company is bad. On Mudaliar's reading of 240 as ruin, the two fit: such men may keep their minds and still lose everything else, as 180 says of the sandal tree in a forest fire.
Both say bad company ruins the good: 179 compares it to a storm wrecking a ship, and 240 to a cobra mating with a viper.

position: The south is the Tamil land, and the verse rebuts a northern claim that those born there cannot reach a good state.
quote: தென்னாடு மிலேச்ச தேசமென்றும், அங்குப் பிறந்தார்க்கு நற்கதியில்லை யென் றுங் கூறும் வடநாட்டார் கொள்கையை மேற்கொண்டு ஓராற்றான் மறுத்தவா றிது

position: The south is Yama's quarter, the direction of death, rather than a region of people.
quote: தென்னாட்டில் (யமதிசையில்) பிறந்த வரும் விண்ணுலகம் அடைவதால்

position: People are simply not like those of their own group; the mind decides.
quote: தங்கள் தங்கள் இனத்தாரை யொத்தவ ரல்லர்

position: People are judged not only by their group but by their minds as well, so group still counts.
quote: தம்தம் இனத்திற்கு ஏற்பமட்டும் இருப்பவரல்லர்; தம்தம் மனத்திற்கு ஏற்பவும் மதிக்கப்படுவர்

note: 773 calls fierceness valour and kindness to a foe who has fallen (ஊராண்மை) its keen edge. 241 says the worthy feel shame to attack a humbled foe.

879 says to cut a thorn tree while it is young, before it can wound the cutter; 241 says the worthy don't attack an enemy at his weakest. Both concern whether to strike a foe while he is weak. The tension holds if 879's thorn tree is an enemy, as Parimelazhagar reads it in the chapter on enmity.

Both use the eclipse snake and the moon. In 148 the moon still lights the world while the snake holds half of it, an image of the nobly born in poverty; in 241 the snake spares the crescent, an image of the worthy sparing a humbled foe.

963 says humility suits prosperity and standing tall suits adversity; 242 says restraint is the ornament of the poor and that living without humility shames one's family. Both concern how the poor should bear themselves. The tension depends on taking 963's உயர்வு as not bowing, as Parimelazhagar glosses it, and 242's அடக்கம் as bowing; if 242 condemns only living beyond one's means, they fit.
125 says humility is good for all and an extra wealth for the rich. 242 makes it the ornament of the poor.
Both deny that origin decides worth: 972 says all are alike in birth and differ by their deeds, and 243 says the next world comes from oneself, not from one's region.
195 calls good and bad caste mere words and puts worth in austerity, learning and effort; 243 makes the same claim about the region of one's birth.

179 says goodness perishes when it comes near bad company, as a storm wrecks a ship; 244 says the good-natured do not turn bad in mind though their company is bad. Both concern whether bad company corrupts the good, and the commentators read 244's இனம் as company, which makes the conflict direct.
458 says that even those with full goodness of mind are strengthened by good company. 244 says the good-natured hold firm without it, even among bad company.

The same image of water leads to opposite claims. 452 says water changes with the soil, so a person's understanding takes on the nature of their company (454 adds that it only seems to be in the mind); 245 says sweet water rises by the sea, so people are as their minds, not their kind. The tension holds if 245's இனம் means the people around one, as the image of surroundings suggests. Shanmuganar's 'not only by their group' softens it.
Both condemn friendship that comes and goes. 215 contrasts the tree flower with the pond flower; 246 says people of steady mind don't leave and rejoin.

168 says parting even from those without discernment brings great pain, so it is best to mix with none; 247 says that parting from the undiscerning is how the pain parts. Both concern whether leaving the undiscerning hurts, and they share the phrase தெரியத் தெரியும் தெரிவிலா. The tension rests on reading 247 as both commentators and Pope do.
Both tie joy to good company and affliction to bad: no greater support than good company and nothing more afflicting than bad (460).
192 says a pliant twig becomes a post for tethering elephants, and so does a life if a man makes himself without slackening; 248 says a person alone raises or lowers himself.
505 makes one's own deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; 248 makes the self the agent of rising and falling.
Both permit the capable to stoop for a purpose: the tiger eats a frog when there is no other meat (193), and the great walk behind the unlearned for a task (249).

967 says it is better to be ruined than to live by following those who scorn you. 249 allows following the unlearned for the sake of a task, which marks a limit on that pride: following for a purpose is not following for a living.
114 names the three ends of life and says gaining the middle one, wealth, brings the other two. 250 pictures a life that completes all three without hindrance, as a ship reaching port.
754 says rightly gained wealth yields virtue and pleasure. 250 counts the life that achieves work, pleasure and virtuous giving together as a voyage completed.
Both call want of understanding the true poverty. Kural 841 adds that the world does not count other lack as lack; 251 adds the image of jewels on one who lacks the essential thing.
Both use a person lacking the marks of a sex to picture a lack that ornament cannot cover: the unlearned wanting to speak (Kural), the senseless rich in their jewels (here).
Both separate wealth from wisdom. The Kural states it as two natures of the world under fate; 252 makes a comic myth of the same fact, the two goddesses quarrelling.
252 explains in jest why Fortune avoids the learned; 266 turns on her and curses her for going to the base and leaving the good.
Both show the unlearned exposed in company. In the Kural his standing wilts as he speaks; here he is asked to read and answers with a stick.

Kural 403 says the unlearned are very good if they can stay silent before the learned; 254 says that even sitting quietly among the wise, such a man is a dog sitting there. Same situation, opposite verdict. The tension holds on Parimelazhagar's plain reading of 403 (silence keeps them from exposure and may lead them to learning), not if 403 is taken as irony.
Both make the fool's mere presence among the worthy a defilement: unwashed feet on a bed (Kural), a dog sitting among them (here).
Both tell those who speak well not to speak in a mean assembly. 255 adds the reason, that the hearers would not take the meaning in, and pictures the low talking freely there.
Both use சோர்வு for the lapse in speech to be guarded against. The Kural says it because gain and ruin come from speech; 256 shows the learned guarding against it by silence.
Good teaching spilt where it is wasted: nectar spilt in a dirty yard (Kural), mango juice pressed into a pig's trough (here).

Both say teaching cannot override what a person already is: in the Kural one's own understanding prevails over many books; here understanding cannot be driven into a body without merit. On the commentators' reading both rest on past deeds.
Both use புன்கோட்டி, the petty assembly. 255 shows the low talking in such assemblies; 260 shows how one is founded, by a man who rejects the learned and finds his like.

Both picture the ungiving man's wealth as a fruiting tree no one can use: a poison tree in the middle of town (Kural), a wood-apple near at hand that the bats ignore (here). Parimelazhagar also stresses that the man is near the poor.
Both picture wealth as drinking water. The Kural's wise man's wealth is the full village tank; here the rich man is the undrinkable sea and the giver the small sweet well.
Both say that being rich and being wise are separate fortunes. 264 makes the sharper point that the senseless live in silk while the wise are passed over.
Kural 169 says the prosperity of the crooked and the ruin of the upright are to be pondered. 265 gives the answer such pondering reaches: the fruit of old deeds, and nothing else.
Both invite wonder at poverty staying with the good and wealth with the unworthy. Neither verse explains it; Parimelazhagar and 265 explain it by past deeds.

Kural 179 says Fortune knows the way and goes to the wise who understand virtue; 266 says she leaves the good and goes to the worthless. Both speak of the goddess choosing whom to join. The tension holds if 179 is a claim about how fortune actually goes, as Parimelazhagar takes it, and not only a promise.
Both say study does not make one learned without understanding: the Kural names that understanding as living in accord with the world.

Both set the sea against a small well. In 263 people seek out the sweet well as they seek out givers; in 275 they wait at a nearly dry well, as the poverty of the worthy is better than wealth that forgets the next world.
Both condemn eating alone to keep one's store full. The Kural ranks it more bitter than begging; 271 shuts the door of the next world on it.
Both reject putting virtue off: the Kural's அன்று அறிவாம் என்னாது ('without saying we'll see to it later') answers the very words of 272's delayers, பின் அறிதும்.
Both describe the man who stores wealth, does not use it and dies: the Kural says he achieved nothing, 273 that his own wealth laughs at him.

Both liken the miser's wealth to a beautiful young woman, with opposite outcomes: in the Kural she grows old alone, unused; here she is enjoyed in due season by a stranger. Unused or lost, the miser has none of it.
Both say that those who neither give nor enjoy have nothing, whatever they hold. 276 makes it a joke in which the speaker owns the miser's wealth as much as he does.
Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty. 277 names troubles poverty spares, but only in comparison with the ungiving rich, so it limits 1041 rather than contradicting it.
274 says the miser's wealth goes to a stranger; 278 follows it to the heirs, who repeat his avarice, so the wealth does no good in either generation.

Both say the base yield only when crushed: like sugar-cane (Kural), like a cow milked by force (here). Both use கொல்ல for the crushing. The Kural's worthy give at a word; here the giver yields like a cow to its calf.

Kural 754 says wealth gained by right means and without wrong yields virtue and pleasure; 280 says wealth at every stage, earning included, is the dwelling of suffering. Both speak of wealth as such and its yield. The tension holds if 280 is about wealth in general, as its wording suggests, and not only the miser's, as the chapter setting might imply.
277 lists the miser's troubles of guarding, burying and clutching; 280 generalizes them into a sequence of earning, guarding, dwindling and loss.

position: The man is poor and unable to help, and is advised to go and live as a guest elsewhere.
quote: ஓர் உதவியுஞ் செய்ய மாட்டாத வறியவன்

position: The man is a miser who gives nothing, and would do better to leave for another place or the other world.
quote: உள்ளூரில் வாழ்ந்தும் ஒன்றும் கொடுக்காத கருமி

note: Both say everyone scorns those who have nothing and honours the rich. 281 adds that noble birth does not help: the penniless are lower than a corpse.

Kural 841 says the world does not count lack of wealth as real lack; 281 says the world counts those who lack it lower than a corpse. Both describe how the world regards the poor. The tension holds on Parimelazhagar's reading of 841's second half as a claim about the world's judgment; Kural 752 sides with 281, so the Kural itself is divided.
Both say the poor lose their own people. Kural 1047 limits it to poverty without virtue, which even a mother treats as a stranger; 283 makes no such exception.
The same bird with opposite morals: the Kural's crows call their kin to share their food, an image of the generous; here crows crowding a carcass are the flatterers round the rich.
Both say poverty destroys the standing of one's ancient family at a stroke. 285 adds valour and learning to what is lost.
Kural 1046 says the words of the poor lose force even when they understand well. 287 goes further: the understanding itself loses its sharpness.

Mudaliar says 288 repeats 286: better to leave the village than live there unable to give. The agreement holds on his reading of 286 as advice to a poor man, not Shanmuganar's reading of it as scorn for a miser.
Both rank begging above a life that does not give: the Kural the hoarder eating alone, 288 the poor man who stays home unable to give.

For the destitute who cannot give, Kural 1050 says the fitting course is to renounce completely, the body included on Parimelazhagar's reading, rather than live off others' salt and gruel. 288 recommends going away and living by begging. Same person, opposite remedies; here the Jain book is the less renunciatory one. The tension depends on Parimelazhagar's reading of 1050.
Both show fallen fortune through food: those who once refused a second helping beg for gruel (1), and hands that wore bracelets cook unsalted greens (289).
The same image and conclusion, bees leaving a flowerless plant and the poor left without kin; Mudaliar notes the repeat.

position: His main reading: what the richer did is the slight they showed, which one does not speak of; he also reports the reading that one fails to proclaim their help.
quote: தம்மினும் மேலான செல்வர்கள் தமக்குச் செய்த எளிமையை

position: The greatest shame is failing to speak gratefully of help one's superiors gave in one's poverty.
quote: தம்மினும் மேலானவர் தமக்குச் செய்த உதவியை நன்றியுடன் வெளியில் சொல்லாதிருப்பதே

note: Both make the honourable mind a fire lit by the rich: a forest fire at their arrogance (291), a forge fire at their contemptuous pity (298).

Both refuse 'going behind' those who scorn (Kural இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று, here இயல்பிலார் பின்சென்று). The Kural says it brings neither praise nor heaven; 292 says the honourable go to those who understand unasked.
Both allow asking before the right people: the Kural finds a beauty in asking those of open heart who know their duty, and 292 sends the honourable to those who grasp the need before it is spoken.
Kural 1057 delights in givers who give without scorn; 293 shows the giver who feeds the poor at the back door with contempt, and draws the matching conclusion: forget such friendship.
Both set an absolute limit: the worthy will not do what brings blame, not to save a starving mother (Kural) and not to save their own lives (here).
Both say the rich who do not give are poor and the poor who do not beg are rich. 296 adds a name for the honourable poor, the great Muttaraiyar.
Both make fear of blame the mark of the highest: the Kural's பழிநாணுவார் see a millet-sized fault as a palmyra; here only blame frightens the best, while lower people fear hunger and pain.
Each book gives honour an animal that dies rather than compromise: the yak that will not live once its hair is gone (Kural), the tiger that starves rather than eat prey fallen on its left (here).
Kural 966 says that following those who scorn you does not lead to the gods' land. 300 goes further: even if heaven were in hand, the excellent would refuse it at honour's cost.
Both ask why a person of worth should stand behind those who look down on him. 966 counts the loss in renown and in heaven; 301 in clear understanding.

656 forbids deeds the wise condemn even to relieve one's mother's hunger. 302 makes the same choice for one's own hunger, and grounds it in the shortness of life rather than in the judgement of the wise.

Both make death and rebirth as brief as an ordinary act of the eyes, and Mudaliar cites 339 here. The Kural uses the image to show impermanence; 302 uses it to make blameless hunger the cheaper choice.
1053 finds a beauty even in asking before unconcealing givers who know their duty. 303 narrows this further: the worthy approach only givers who first welcome them in, so asking becomes hospitality.
963 asks for dignity when circumstances shrink; 304 shows it, with fortune and the gods both gone and the worthy still refusing to bow to the hoarding rich.
The first half restates 1061: not asking even of givers dear as one's eyes, who give without holding back, is far better. Both use the same phrase, கண்ணன்னார்.
Both have the heart melt (உள்ளம் உருகும்) at the thought of begging. 1069 goes on to the one who refuses; 305 to the beggar at the moment of taking.

Both reject begging as a cure for poverty. In Parimelazhagar's reading the Kural's alternative is effort; 306's is to want less and consent to hardship. They differ on the remedy, not on the refusal, and the difference shows the Naladiyar's turn toward renunciation.

1057 speaks of beggars rejoicing when they meet givers who give without scorn, which assumes such givers exist. 307 says the man who does not scorn beggars has never been born. The conflict holds only if 307 is taken literally; Mudaliar's explanations treat it as overstatement or wordplay.
In both, the asker's life goes out at the word of refusal. 1070 turns the point against the refuser; 308 stays with the asker.
1066 finds nothing more degrading to the tongue than asking, even for water for a cow. 309 also places the disgrace in the spoken request rather than in dependence.
803 asks what use old friendship is if a friend's liberties aren't accepted as one's own. On Shanmuganar's reading, 310 shows the cost of that failure to the friend who relied on it.

position: The four are a method of disputation: breadth raises objections, subtlety answers them, and the remainder states the conclusion they establish.
quote: எச்சவுரையாவது இவ்வாறு தடைவிடைகளான் முடிந்த ஒரு பொருளை யுரைத்தல்.

position: The remainder is research that brings out what lies hidden and unsaid in the text.
quote: நூலில் எஞ்சி மறைந்து கிடப்பதை எடுத்துக்கூறும் ஆராய்ச்சியுரை

position: Those of low birth lack the restraint needed to protect others' words from scorn.
quote: பிறருடைய சொற்களை (இகழாமற்) காத்தற்குரிய (அடக்கம் முதலிய) சாதனமுடையவரோ?

position: Those of low birth cannot protect and care for others by what they say.
quote: தம் சொல்லால், பிறரைப் போற்றிக் காக்கத்தக்க கருவி போன்றிருப்பரோ?

note: Both tell those who speak well in a good assembly not to speak in a mean one; 311 describes the mean assembly in detail.
312 warns that the bad scholar will rise to fight; 315 shows the cost to whoever stays to argue: his teeth in his hand.
649 says those who cannot say a few faultless words long to say many; 313 shows the same many-worded speaker in debate.
403 says even the unlearned are good if they stay silent before the learned; 314's fool fails at exactly that.
857 says those of bitter understanding who hold to hostility do not see the truth that brings victory; 315's disputants want victory and will not accept the truth (மெய் கொள்ளார்).
In 69 a mother rejoices more than at his birth when she hears her son called சான்றோன். In 316 the சான்றோர் themselves grieve for the mother of a fool. The two verses are mirror images.
317 separates a book's text from its meaning; 318 separates those who keep the text from those who grasp the meaning and teach it.
650 likens those who cannot explain what they learned to flowers without scent; 318 sets them apart from scholars who make others understand.
318 says true scholars make a book's meaning clear to others; 319 sets out what that explanation must contain.

409 says the learned of low birth have a worth the unlearned of high birth lack. 320 says that however much they learn, those without good birth cannot do what the well-born do. The conflict depends on reading இற்பிறப்பு as birth into a good family, as both commentators do, and on counting the capacity 320 denies as part of the worth 409 gives to learning.
992 makes birth in a good family one of the two parts of courtesy; 320 credits good birth with the restraint to overlook another's petty understanding.
Both use milk-rice whose taste goes unknown: the ladle that stirs it and the dog that prefers leather.
415 makes the words of the good a staff on slippery ground; in 321 the learned value such words while the fool mocks them.
Both describe hearing that isn't hearing: 418's ear unpierced by instruction is deaf though it hears, and 322's listeners lend an ear and still do not hear (செவிகொடுத்தும் கேட்கலார்).
Both end on the same verdict, 'what matter whether they die or live'. The Kural aims it at those who taste with the mouth and not the ear; 323 at those who see death coming and do no good.
999 says the world is dark even by day for those who cannot laugh with others; 324 asks why anyone would refuse to smile with those he meets.
158 tells one to defeat those who wrong one out of arrogance by one's own forbearance; 325 shows that defeat in public, though it doesn't name forbearance.
