326 shows the cost of putting off virtue until old age; 332 names the usual excuse, that the household's needs come first.
1006 names the same two failures, not using one's wealth and not giving to the deserving. 327 adds a third: not taking the good path that protects.
Both picture the end, when the tongue no longer works. 335 urges good deeds before that moment; 328 shows the gesture that comes too late.
Both mock the words of postponement: பின்னறிவாம் here, மற்றறிவாம் in 332.
333 says wealth doesn't stay, so do lasting deeds as soon as you have it. 329 shows people who think of such deeds only when their means are gone.
336 states the general fact that one here yesterday is gone today. 330 makes it the death of one's own loved ones and still finds people unmoved.

position: உலகம் means the worlds to be reached after this life, heaven and release, so what the fool lacks is knowledge of what leads there.
quote: உலகம்- (மறுமையில் அடையத்தக்க சுவர்க்க மோக்ஷம் என்னும்) உலகங்களின் தகுதியை.

position: உலகம் means the ways of the world, and what the fool lacks is knowledge of how to live by them.
quote: பழம் பெருஞ் சிறப் புடைய உலக நடைமுறையை அறியாது ஒழுகுதல்

note: 337 mocks those who cannot know they will live another moment yet plan in crores; 331's turtle is a picture of that ignorance.
36 says to do virtue without saying 'we'll see to it then' (அன்றறிவாம்); 332 mocks the household version of the same words (மற்றறிவாம்).

On Shanmuganar's reading the two make the same claim: learning without knowing how to live with the world is still ignorance. On Mudaliar's reading, where உலகம் is the worlds after death, the link does not hold.
Both compare a person without human quality to an inert thing, a tree in 997 and a stone in 334. 334 goes further and ranks the stone above the person for its usefulness.
Both put the fool's urge to speak in an itching tongue (சுனை): in 313 the itch to debate, here the itch to abuse.
Both warn against following those who do not accept you. 967 counts the cost in honour; 336 in futility.
304 says the worthy will not stand behind the hoarding rich; 337 says people at large do. 304 describes the exception to 337's rule.
Both list the goods a fool's life lacks: 327 enjoyment, giving and the good path; 338 adds love and renown.
816 rates being a stranger to the wise far above close friendship with a fool; 339 says friendship with the undiscerning is painful even if it brought the whole earth.
978 says smallness adorns itself in self-admiration; 340 shows the self-praiser mocked as mad.

position: With prosperity the base man becomes adept at a conduct different from his earlier one.
quote: வற்றாம் ஒரு நடை- (முன்னைய நடைக்கு வேறாகிய) ஒரு நடக்கையின் வல்லவனாவன்;

position: With prosperity the base man keeps to his own low course.
quote: தனது தாழ்ந்த ஒரு போக்கையே பின்பற்ற வல்லவனாம்.

note: Both say study does not override what a person already is. In Parimelazhagar's reading 373 credits the lasting understanding to fate; 341 credits it to base nature.
Both use a domestic animal that keeps its habit despite good feeding: the hen to its rubbish heap, the dog to others' leftovers.
976 says the small have no thought of cherishing the great and taking them as guides; 342 shows the base man inventing excuses not to go to them.
On Shanmuganar's reading 343 matches 973: being placed high does not make the base high, nor does it change the worthy.
On Mudaliar's reading, prosperity turns the base man to a new course, as 977 says distinction falling to the unworthy turns into excess.
The first half restates 104 with the same millet and palm, and Mudaliar cites it here.
105 says a benefit's measure is the worth of the one who receives it; 344's second half shows that measure at zero, with palm-sized help counting for nothing among the ungrateful.
978 says greatness always bows and smallness admires itself; 346 shows both, with an emperor's wealth on one side and a fraction of a coin on the other.
963 asks for humility in abundance; 346's worthy keep it even with an emperor's wealth.
505 makes one's deeds the touchstone of greatness and smallness; 347 and 350 apply it to the base who have grown rich, whose wealth cannot hide what their deeds show.
1079's base man finds fault on seeing others well fed and clothed; 348's rejoices when others suffer. They are the same envy seen from both sides.
810 praises those who do not change toward old friends; 349 gives the worthy that constancy and shows the base without it.
The two share their closing lines word for word: 347 makes the point with an object, the jewelled sandal, and 350 with an animal, the young bullocks.

position: இறப்பர் means the courtesans leave a man once they have taken all his wealth; the verse is an allegory of fools who praise themselves to get money.
quote: அறிவிலார் தம்மைப்பிறர் நன்கு மதிக்கும்படி தம்மைத்தாமே புகழ்ந்து பேசிப் பொருள் பறிப்பரென்பதூ

position: இறப்பர் means they overstep all bounds, rating themselves highly; he reads the verse as a contrast between the women themselves.
quote: தம்மைப் பெரிதாய் மதித்து வரம்பு கடந்து செல்வர்.

note: Both say study does not change what a person is: 823 says the unworthy rarely become good at heart however many good books they learn, and 352 says those without fine discernment never gain it from flawless books.

184 ranks harsh words to a man's face above careless words behind his back. 353 doesn't let face-to-face speech off: the base are shameless precisely because they list a man's faults standing beside him.
On Mudaliar's reading of 354 as a figure, both make self-display the mark of the small: 978 says smallness adorns itself in self-admiration, and 354's wantons adorn and vaunt themselves.
Both say the base give only to force: 1077's base won't shake their wet hands except for those who would break their jaws, and 355's chisel only moves when struck.
1078's sugar-cane yields only when crushed, and 355's chisel cuts only when struck: two tools of labour for the same claim about the base.
108 tells one to keep a good done in mind and forget the bad that very day. 356 says the worthy do exactly this and the base do the reverse, dwelling on abuse.

Both make one kindness outweigh great injury: in 109 a wrong as painful as killing vanishes at the thought of one good, and in 357 the worthy bear a hundred faults for one kindness. 357 adds the base, for whom the scale runs the other way.
955 says an old family doesn't part from its nature even when its means shrink, and 358 says the well-born do in poverty what the base won't do in wealth.
Both mock plans made without regard to life's shortness: 337's unwise think crores of thoughts without knowing they'll live a moment more, and 359's dreamers say 'today, now, soon' and perish.

Both picture people who have the means of feeling and none of the feeling: 576's men have eyes but no kind regard and are like trees in the soil, and 360's rich live in wealth but stay dry as the netti's pith.

position: He reads the condition as 'even if they get no chance to stray': strict guard can stop the deed, but most women's minds still go astray.
quote: மகளிர் கடுங்காவலின் வைகிக் குற்றஞ் செய்தற்குச் சிறிது மிடம் பெறாராயினும் அவர் மனந் தீவழிச் செல்லுதலே பெரும்பான்மை

position: He keeps the condition as written: the claim applies if women take the faulty way.
quote: தாம் இழுக்கான வழியில் செல்வா ராயின்

note: 53 asks what is lacking if the wife has worth and what is present if she lacks it. 361 gives the second half a picture: every grandeur present, and the house a wilderness.
Both say guards can't keep women chaste. 57 concludes that a woman's own steadfastness is the best guard; 362, on Mudaliar's reading, doubts that most women have it.
52 says a life has nothing if the wife lacks household excellence. 363 names three such failings and calls each a weapon that kills the husband.

46 asks what one gains by leaving a virtuous household life for the ascetic's way. 364 calls returning to married life a fault like stoning oneself, and Mudaliar takes it as the wise telling one to give household life up. The tension holds on Mudaliar's reading; if the verse is only about remarriage after a wife's death, as Shanmuganar's gloss allows, it is narrower.
56 explains why the learned call marriage கடி, a dread; 364 opens by citing that name, and Mudaliar points back to 56.

47 puts the one who lives household life according to its nature first among all who strive; 365 puts austerity first and household life in the middle. Parimelazhagar limits 47's 'all who strive' to those in the third stage, not full renunciants, which softens the conflict.
Two ranked lists of lives side by side. Both put enjoyment of what one has in the middle and craving at the bottom, but the top changes from austerity to learning.
Both use the sprout to read what lies behind it: in 959 the sprout shows the soil as speech shows the lineage, and in 367 the paddy breeds true as a son's mind follows his father's.
169 calls the prosperity of the crooked and the ruin of the upright a thing to ponder. 368 describes that world: the worthy fallen and the base risen, the umbrella turned upside down.
788 says friendship removes distress at once, like a hand catching a slipping garment. 369 says a heart that doesn't respond so is not worth keeping alive.
The same frame, word for word in places, with two images of a love that lasts only while it is fed: the flood that ends with the rain, and the lamp that ends with the oil.

position: தாம் ஆர்ந்தபோது refers to the men: when, now poor, they come of their own desire, the women turn harsh.
quote: தாம் ஆர்ந்தபோது - (வறுமையடைந்து) தாமே விரும்பிச் சென்ற போது.

position: It refers to the women: once they are filled with a man's wealth, they turn harsh.
quote: தாம் செல்வம் நிரம்பியபோது இனிமையற்றவராய்

position: The dupes themselves examine and know the guile, yet don't grasp that the women should be shunned.
quote: (அவர் பரிகரிக்கத் தக்காரென்று) உணரார்கள்.

position: The world knows the guile clearly; the sinful fools alone don't know it.
quote: உலகினரால் தெளிவாக அறியப்பட்டிருந்தும் பாவம் நிறைந்த உடம்பை யுடைய மூடர் அறியமாட்டார்.

note: 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth, not the man, bring harm. 371 gives the mechanism: their love burns only while the money feeds it.
Both are the dupe's own speech recalling a vow of inseparable love, a death pact in 372 and a promise never to part in 376, broken when his money ran out.
912's women weigh the profit before they speak of their virtue; 374's women weigh only wealth, so the poor man is poison and the oil-presser with money is sugar.
920 names இருமனப் பெண்டிர், double-minded women, among the company of the ruined; 375's eel, showing one face to the snake and another to the fish, pictures the double mind.
Both use the fighting ram's horn, which twists away, for the courtesan's love turned to hostility.

918 says the embrace of deceiving women is an அணங்கு to those without discernment; 377's wild cow, whose lick pleases and then kills in Mudaliar's gloss, is the same danger, with public ridicule added.

914 says those who seek the wealth of grace won't touch the base charms of women who count only wealth; 378 says those who mean to reach the right path won't embrace them, which Mudaliar takes as the path to liberation.
913 compares the false embrace to holding a stranger's corpse in a dark room; 379 says the women belong to no one but their bodies. Both deny that anyone is present in the embrace.
917 says those without firmness of heart embrace women whose hearts are on other things; 380 says those full of sin don't grasp the guile of women whose minds are with another man.

On the commentators' reading, both place a wife's chastity in her own keeping: 57 calls the guard of her own steadfastness the best, and 381 praises the woman whose conduct leaves no one pursuing her. On Pope's reading, 381 instead credits the absence of temptation.
51's good wife lives within her husband's means; 382's good wife keeps her duties of hospitality even when the means are one pot of water and the guests could drink the sea.

The two halves of one claim: 361's mansion without a good wife is a wilderness, and 383's leaking hut with one is the only true home. Mudaliar's gloss on 383, that other houses are forests, makes the pairing explicit.
1302 says sulking is right in measure like salt and spoils if prolonged; 384's good wife sulks at the right moment and relents sweetly.

385's wife never loses her shyness with her husband however often they meet; 1257's woman knows nothing of shame when her beloved does what she desires. The second describes desire overriding reserve after separation, so the two set limits on each other rather than conflict.
Both wives refuse a chest that other women have shared: 1311 because all women feast on him with their eyes, and 387 because he comes from the courtesans unbathed.
The same speech to the minstrel in the same frame, with two images of the neglected side: the unstruck face of the drum and the sapless end joints of the sugar-cane.
Both wives read the courtesans' embraces on the husband's chest, unwashed in 387 and smeared with sandal in 389.
Both make sulking love's salt: 1302 measures it, with too much spoiling the dish, and 391 says love without it has no salt at all.
1306 says love without quarrels, serious and light, is like over-ripe or unripe fruit; 391 says that union and sulking together are love's way.
The good wife of 384 sulks at the right moment and relents sweetly; 391 gives the reason, that without sulking love has no salt.
In both, a sound of the season becomes a killing instrument for the separated woman: the rain's thunder is a funeral drum in 392, and the herdsman's flute a weapon in 1228.

The funeral drum appears in both: in 364 it should teach a man to give up married life, and in 392 the thunder sounds like it to a woman whose husband is away. The same sound serves renunciation in one book and love in the other.
Both make evening the bewildering hour of separation: 393's மம்மர்கொள் மாலை, and 1229's evening that confuses the mind of the whole town.
Two evening scenes in one frame: the day's work falls silent, and the woman casts off her garland and weeps for the absent man.
Both have the woman count the days of absence on her fingers, and Mudaliar cites 1261 with 394. In 1261 she speaks; in 394 the man imagines it.
Both make her brow a bow that guards her eyes: in 1086 the brows, if they would only screen her eyes, would spare him his pain, and in 395 they frighten off the kingfisher.
The mother of 396 doubts that feet which shrank from soft dye can bear the stony path; the girl of 398 answers that the strength comes with the man, as riding comes with the horse.
Both are the mother's speech after her daughter's flight: 396 fears for the girl's feet on the way, and 399 rereads the farewell embrace she didn't understand.

1225's woman asks what she did to morning and to evening, looking for the cause of her pain in the hours. 400 runs through such suspects and acquits them, blaming only the road her lover took for wealth.
